name: Cortexin
lead: Cortexin is a neuroprotective peptide medicine made by the Russian company Geropharm from the cerebral cortex of cattle. It is given by intramuscular injection and used mainly in Russia and some post-Soviet countries for neurological conditions such as cerebrovascular disorders, head injury effects, encephalopathies and developmental delay in children.[1]

Cortexin is not marketed for appearance. It reaches looksmaxxing-adjacent circles through the nootropic and peptide-stack conversation, where people interested in focus, memory and mental performance look at it among brain-directed peptides. Any link to looks is therefore indirect and rests on how people use it for cognitive goals rather than on a cosmetic claim.

Research on it is mostly Russian-language: a multicenter randomized study of dose-dependent effects in chronic cerebral ischemia, trials in children with head injury and neuropsychiatric conditions, and rat studies in brain ischemia.[2][3][7][8][9] Cochrane's review of the related product Cerebrolysin, not Cortexin, addresses acute stroke.[4]

paras: Grokipedia describes Cortexin as a lyophilisate of low-molecular water-soluble polypeptide fractions from bovine cerebral cortex, with molecular weights of 1 to 10 kDa.[1] A Russian review describes it as an animal cortex extract containing neuropeptides, amino acids and trace elements.[5]

The product is supplied as a lyophilisate that is dissolved before intramuscular injection, and Grokipedia states that Geropharm is the sole manufacturer of the original product using a proprietary extraction technology.[1] Cortexin is a branded animal-derived drug and is distinct from the cortexin gene family of neuron-specific membrane proteins identified in rodent cortex in the 1990s, which shares the name but not the product.[17]

The Russian review proposes that its components act on molecular targets in neuronal signaling at several stages of pathology.[5] Grokipedia lists neuroprotective, neurotrophic and neuronal-function-restoring actions, including effects on antioxidant systems and neurotrophic factors; this is AI-generated and unverified.[1]

Grokipedia states that the effects include modulation of excitatory and inhibitory amino-acid metabolism, antioxidant action, inhibition of neuronal apoptosis and stimulation of neurite growth via factors such as BDNF and NGF; as an AI-generated source, this is listed as the manufacturer-style description rather than as independently confirmed.[1] A 2023 study in cultured rat sensory neurons reported that Cortexin ameliorated high-glucose-induced neuropathy in vitro.[13]

A multicenter randomized controlled study published in a Russian journal in 2018 examined dose-dependent effects of Cortexin in chronic cerebral ischemia.[3] Earlier, a 1999 trial in 76 patients with stage I-II dyscirculatory encephalopathy compared standard therapy (31 patients) with standard therapy plus Cortexin delivered by nasal electrophoresis (45 patients), assessing clinical symptoms, psychophysiological tests and EEG.[8] A 2006 randomized comparative study examined several neuroprotectors in ischemic stroke.[9]

In children, a controlled clinical study enrolled 74 patients aged 6 to 13 with moderate brain contusion treated in outpatient clinics, assessed with neurological examination, EEG, CT and psychological testing.[7] A 2011 controlled study examined Cortexin for memory disorders in children,[11] and a 2024 randomized trial examined rehabilitation measures using Cortexin in children with neuropsychiatric pathology.[10] A Russian review of tics and Tourette's syndrome in children describes local experience treating tics with hopantenic acid, topiramate and Cortexin neuropeptides.[16] A 2007 controlled study in healthy volunteers examined meteoadaptogenic properties of peptide drugs, and a 2024 observational study examined post-stroke cognitive impairment in young patients.[12][14]

These are mainly Russian-language studies from regional centres; no trial has examined Cortexin for appearance outcomes. Studies of related products exist: a Cochrane review of Cerebrolysin in acute ischaemic stroke,[4] and a blinded comparison of Cerebrolysin and other peptide preparations in embolic stroke.[6]
A 2021 PLoS ONE study compared Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and Actovegin in rat models of acute and chronic brain ischemia over 10 days, the first comparison of the three.[2]

Cortexin is a prescription drug in Russia and neighbouring countries, where it is used in neurology, paediatrics and rehabilitation, and is part of a family of peptide bioregulators and animal-tissue preparations (such as Cerebrolysin and Actovegin) that are widely prescribed in the region but less familiar in Western practice.[1][2] It is discussed by some in nootropic communities as an import, but no detailed community discussion was available for this article.

card.summary: A Russian cattle-brain peptide injection used for neurological conditions, with some local trials and no appearance data.

quick.overview:
Cortexin is a cattle-brain-cortex peptide complex made by Geropharm and prescribed in Russia and nearby countries for neurological conditions.
It is occasionally described as a nootropic, but has no documented use for appearance. Evidence is a Russian randomized study and rat ischemia models.
quick.mechanism: It is proposed to act as a neuroprotective and neurotrophic peptide mixture; an animal study showed protective effects in brain ischemia.
quick.risks: Safety information is limited. It is an animal-derived injectable available by prescription in Russia.

chain: Used in clinical practice for brain-injury and cerebrovascular conditions
Discussed by some users as a nootropic; no direct appearance claim
angle.text: Cortexin has no appearance claim of its own. People who discuss it do so as a nootropic peptide for memory and mental performance, and its medical use in Russia is for neurological conditions.
